# 2 Chronicles 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

The chapter describes the furnishings and utensils Solomon made for the temple: the bronze altar, the Sea (great basin), ten smaller basins, ten gold lampstands, ten tables, the courts, and the extensive bronze work of Huram (Hiram), followed by a summary of golden furnishings. The parallel account is found in 1 Kings 7.

---

## v. 1 — The Bronze Altar

- **"He made a bronze altar…"** The Hebrew word for altar essentially means "killing-place" — the place of sacrifice, the center of worship for priests and people. David Guzik notes the spiritual parallel: "Our altar — our 'killing-place' — is the cross, where Jesus died for our sins and we die to self and live for Jesus" (Hebrews 13:10). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Size:** Twenty cubits square (about 30 feet / 9–10 meters) and ten cubits high (about 15 feet / 4.5 meters). This was roughly four times the square area of the tabernacle altar (Exodus 27:1, which was five cubits square and three cubits high). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Why so large?** Matthew Henry explains that God had "greatly enlarged their borders" and it was fitting they should enlarge His altars. The height (about 15 feet) meant the people in the courts could see the sacrifice being burnt, and "their eye might affect their heart with sorrow for sin." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Not in Kings:** Ellicott notes this verse is not found in the parallel chapters of 1 Kings 6–7 describing the temple construction, though the altar is incidentally mentioned in 1 Kings 9:25 and implied in 1 Kings 8:22, 64. The Hebrew style matches the older document, suggesting the verse was accidentally omitted from the text of Kings. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **First item:** The Pulpit Commentary observes that the altar is the first item mentioned in the list of furniture leading to the ark. "In New Testament terms, we could say that the way to the throne of God begins at the cross." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Catholic view (Haydock):** Notes that a sloping ascent was made up to the altar according to Josephus, or the steps were enclosed (see Exodus 20:26 forbidding steps). The inside of the altar may have been filled with earth or rough stones, though this is uncertain for the brazen altar. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Gill:** Questions whether the altar was only covered with brass (like Moses') or made of solid ("massy") brass. It was four times as big in square as Moses' altar and three times higher plus a cubit. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/4.htm]
- **Trapp:** "That all the people might see the burnt-offerings, and be reminded of their sins and of their Saviour; for the ceremonial law was their gospel." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]

---

## v. 2 — The Sea of Cast Metal

- **"Sea of cast metal…circular in shape, measuring ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits in height, and thirty cubits in circumference."** This enormous bronze basin—over 15 feet (4.5 m) in diameter and 7.5 feet (2.25 m) high—replaced the tabernacle's bronze laver (Exodus 30:18). It was called a "sea" on account of its great size. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Use:** The Sea was for the priests to wash in (v. 6). Priests who failed to wash would die (Exodus 30:20), emphasizing the necessity of purification before approaching God. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Pi and biblical accuracy:** Critics have claimed a mathematical error because a circle of 10 cubits diameter should have a circumference of about 31.416 cubits (not 30). The *Defender's Study Bible* responds that the dimensions are round numbers using the principle of "significant figures" — a diameter of "10" means between 9.5 and 10.5, and circumference "30" means between 29.5 and 30.5, giving a range for π between 2.81 and 3.21. The precise value of π falls within that range. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The diameter and circumference "harmonize, of course, to all practical purposes." It also asks whether the circumference was measured at the rim or around the girth (belly), which would affect calculations of volume. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/4-2.htm]
- **Typology:** John Olley notes that "the calm water in the large 'sea' reminded worshipers of the Lord's rule over all creation and history." In Ezekiel's temple and the New Jerusalem, there is no standing container of water — instead a river of life (Ezekiel 47:1-12; Revelation 22:1-2). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Hebrew text:** Ellicott notes the verse is word-for-word identical with 1 Kings 7:23 except for one differing preposition. The Hebrew uses *qāw* for "measuring-line," while Kings has the rare form *qāwèh*. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Gaebelein's typology:** The Sea is "typical of that cleansing which His people need and which is so graciously provided by the Lord Himself." The immense quantity of water "suggests the unlimited provision grace has made." In Revelation 4:6 the sea before the throne is of glass like crystal — because the redeemed in glory "do no longer need cleansing." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 3 — Figures of Oxen Below the Rim

- **"Figures of oxen encircled it, ten per cubit…cast in two rows."** This is one of the notable textual differences between Chronicles and Kings. 1 Kings 7:24 reads "gourds" (*peqa'im*, wild gourds or colocynths) instead of "oxen" (*beqarim*). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Textual debate (Ellicott):** The Hebrew words for "oxen" and "gourds" could easily be confused by a transcriber. Most commentators assume the text of Chronicles has suffered corruption and should be restored from Kings. However, Ellicott argues there is no reason the ornamental rows could not have included *both* features — small oxen figures as well as wild gourds. The diminutive size ("ten per cubit") was "by no means beyond the resources of ancient art." It is "sheer dogmatism to assert that 'the copyists have absurdly changed the gourds into oxen.'" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Haydock (Catholic):** Observes that "ten in a cubit" on a thirty-cubit circumference with two rows would mean 600 oxen heads. Others suppose only five in each row. The Septuagint and Syriac omit this verse. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 4 — The Sea Stood on Twelve Oxen

- **"Three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east…all their hindquarters toward the center."** The twelve oxen supported the great basin. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Typological interpretation (Trapp, cited by Guzik):** The twelve oxen "prefigured the twelve apostles, who carried the water of life all the world over." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Alternative symbolism (John Olley):** The twelve oxen facing the four compass directions provide "an image of strength covering all the earth," and "may also represent the twelve tribes of Israel, which in the wilderness encamped around the tabernacle" (Numbers 2:1-31). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Ellicott:** The whole verse coincides verbally with 1 Kings 7:25, with only the form of the numeral "twelve" differing slightly. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 5 — Handbreadth Thick; Three Thousand Baths

- **"It was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom."** The thickness (about 3–4 inches) and the decorative lily-blossom rim are noted. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Three thousand baths vs. two thousand baths:** A well-known discrepancy with 1 Kings 7:26, which says "two thousand baths." Several explanations have been proposed:
  - **Adam Clarke (via Guzik):** Since Chronicles was written after the Babylonian exile, it may refer to the Babylonian bath, which was smaller than the ancient Jewish bath. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
  - **Matthew Henry:** If filled to the brim, it held 3,000 baths; ordinarily there were only 2,000 baths in it. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
  - **Jewish Targum:** "It received 3,000 baths of dry measure, and held 2,000 of liquid measure." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
  - **Defender's Study Bible:** If it could receive 3,000 baths, it could certainly contain 2,000 — both statements can be true as they stand. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
  - **Believer's Study Bible:** Suggests scribal inadvertency — perhaps an error during transmission caused by the repetition of the numeral "three" four times in v. 4. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
  - **Ellicott:** Most critics assume Kings is correct; a scribe may have read *'alāphîm* ("thousands") instead of *'alpayim* ("two thousand"), then added "three" under the influence of the previous verse. But it is also possible "three" was inadvertently omitted from Kings. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
  - **Haydock (Catholic):** 3 Kings (1 Kings) says "two" — this may "specify the usual quantity that was contained, though the vessel would absolutely hold a thousand measures, or baths, more." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **NET Notes:** A bath was roughly 6 gallons (about 22 liters); 3,000 baths ≈ 18,000 gallons (66,000 liters). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Typology (Matthew Henry):** The Sea signified two things: (1) "Our great gospel privilege, that the blood of Christ cleanseth from all sin" (1 John 1:7) — a fountain opened for all believers; (2) "Our great gospel duty, which is to cleanse ourselves by true repentance." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]

---

## v. 6 — Ten Basins for Washing

- **"Ten basins…five on the south side and five on the north."** The smaller basins (*kiyyorim*) were used for rinsing the parts of the burnt offerings — washing the animal pieces and utensils involved in sacrifice. The Sea was reserved exclusively for the priests' ceremonial washing. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Distinction in function:** J. A. Thompson notes this distinction in use between the basins and the Sea is highlighted by the Chronicler. The parallel in 1 Kings 7 is longer, including a detailed description of the portable stands (vv. 27–37) that the Chronicler omits. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Ellicott:** The Chronicler deliberately abbreviates, omitting the description of the ten bases/stands because of their "unusual difficulty" or because he considered them of less importance. The statement about the different uses of the basins and the Sea is "peculiar to the chronicler." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Priestly washing:** GotQuestions.org explains that the bronze laver/Sea was the last object encountered before entering the sanctuary (Exodus 40:6-7). Before entering God's presence, one must be cleansed — a requirement fulfilled finally in Christ's blood (Hebrews 1:3). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]

---

## v. 7 — Ten Gold Lampstands

- **"Ten gold lampstands according to their specifications…five on the south side and five on the north."** The tabernacle had only one golden lampstand (menorah); the temple had ten. David Guzik notes this "fittingly displayed a greater light and a greater dynamic of fellowship" than the tabernacle era. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **"According to their specifications":** The Pulpit Commentary explains this phrase means "according to the prescribed ordinance" — the pattern originally given for the tabernacle lampstand (Exodus 25:31) was followed, just multiplied. [https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/4.htm]
- **Ellicott:** "According to their rule, or prescribed manner" — the Vulgate renders it *secundum speciem quâ jussa erant fieri* ("according to the form which they were commanded to be made"). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Gaebelein:** The increase from one to ten lampstands (and tables) foreshadows "that coming glorious Kingdom of Christ. Then there will be the increase and the blessing typified by the ten lavers, the ten candlesticks and the ten tables." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 8 — Ten Tables and a Hundred Gold Bowls

- **"Ten tables…five on the south side and five on the north…a hundred gold bowls."** Again, the tabernacle had one table of showbread; the temple had ten — representing expanded fellowship with God. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **The bowls:** J. Barton Payne notes the "sprinkling bowls" were used "for collecting the blood of sacrifices, which was then sprinkled about the altar in the temple services of atonement." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Ellicott:** The ten tables are not mentioned in the parallel narrative of 1 Kings, which speaks of only one table of showbread (1 Kings 7:48). The Chronicler consistently speaks of plural tables (also 1 Chronicles 28:16 and 2 Chronicles 4:19), while elsewhere he himself speaks of "the Pure Table" as if there were only one (2 Chronicles 13:11; 29:18). The difficulty "cannot be solved with certainty," but Ellicott suggests the Chronicler may have grouped multiple tables together with the Table of Showbread for brevity. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 9 — The Courtyard of the Priests and the Large Court

- **"The courtyard of the priests and the large court with its doors…overlaid…with bronze."** The temple had two courts:
  - **Inner court** (court of the priests): open only to priests. Enclosed by a wall of hewn stones and cedar beams (1 Kings 6:36). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
  - **Outer court** (the great court): open to all Israel. The Hebrew word *'azārâh* is a late term, common in the Targums. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Typological significance:** Guzik, citing Payne, notes: "This very division into two courts gave concrete expression to the fact that under the older testament there had not yet been achieved that universal priesthood of the believers that would come about through Jesus Christ. In him all the people of God have direct access to the Father." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Ellicott:** This section is peculiar to Chronicles. The outer court is not mentioned in the parallel narrative of Kings. The bronze-plated doors reflect ancient Near Eastern practice — Shalmaneser's palace doors at Balawat were 22 feet high with bronze overlay. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 10 — The Sea Placed on the South Side, Southeast Corner

- **Position:** "He put the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner." Ellicott renders the Hebrew literally: "on the right shoulder, eastward, in front of the southward" — i.e., the south-east side of the temple house. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- This matches 1 Kings 7:39 and places the great basin in the southeastern part of the inner court, between the altar and the temple entrance — following the pattern of the tabernacle where the laver stood between altar and sanctuary. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]

---

## vv. 11–16 — Huram's Bronze Work

- **"Huram made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls."** Huram (also called Hiram in Kings) was the master craftsman from Tyre — half-Israelite and half-Gentile (2 Chronicles 2:13-14) — responsible for the fine artistic metalwork. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Why the Chronicler emphasizes these items:** Selman notes that "the emphasis on the temple vessels…underlines the continuity represented by the temple. The return of the temple vessels to the second temple was one of the chief signs that post-exilic Israel remained a worshipping community of covenant people (cf. Ezra 1:7-11; 6:5; 8:24-34)." These were among the few articles from Solomon's temple recovered and reused after the exile. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **"Pots":** Ellicott explains these were "scuttles for carrying away the ashes of the altar." The Hebrew word differs by a single stroke from "lavers" in 1 Kings 7:40. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **The two pillars (v. 12):** These are Jachin and Boaz, described more fully in 1 Kings 7:15-22. The "bowl-shaped capitals" (*gullōth*, globes) and the network (*sebākhōth*, lattices) decorated the tops of the pillars. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Four hundred pomegranates (v. 13):** Two rows of pomegranates for each network covering the capitals. These decorative elements appear also in the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:33-34). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **The stands and basins (v. 14):** Ellicott notes the repetition of "he made" is suspicious; Kings shows the correct reading: "the bases ten, and the lavers ten upon the bases." The Hebrew for "ten" closely resembles "he made." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **"Huram-abi" (v. 16):** The term *'ābî* (father) is a title of honor meaning "master" or "master craftsman," not a biological relationship (see 2 Chronicles 2:13). All the bronze articles were of "polished" (*mārûq*) bronze. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 17 — Cast in Clay Molds in the Plain of the Jordan

- **"Between Succoth and Zeredah."** This location was east of the Jordan River, roughly halfway between the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee. Andrew Hill notes this placed the casting operation "a considerable distance from the source of copper used in the bronze casting if it was mined at Timnah." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **"Clay molds":** Hebrew "in the thickness of the ground" — referring to the stiff, clayey soil of the Jordan Valley suitable for making casting molds. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Zeredah/Zarethan:** The names denote the same place (Joshua 3:16; 1 Kings 11:26). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 18 — The Weight of the Bronze Could Not Be Determined

- **"Solomon made all these articles in such great abundance that the weight of the bronze could not be determined."** F. B. Meyer is cited by Guzik: "This was as it should be. There was no attempt to keep an accurate account of what was given to the service of God…There is a tendency in all of us to keep a strict account of what we give to God…but the loftiest form of devotion overleaps such calculation." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Ellicott:** The Kings parallel reads, "Solomon left all the vessels unweighed from very great abundance." The Chronicler may have substituted an easier term, missing the nuance of the verb in Kings, or a copyist's eye may have wandered to the beginning of the next verse. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 19 — The Golden Altar and Tables for the Bread of the Presence

- **"The golden altar; the tables on which was placed the Bread of the Presence."** The "golden altar" is the altar of incense, equivalent to that in the Mosaic tabernacle (Exodus 30:1-10). It stood in the Holy Place before the veil leading to the Most Holy Place. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **Tables (plural):** As in v. 8, the Chronicler speaks of multiple tables while 1 Kings 7:48 mentions a single table. Ellicott suggests the Chronicler grouped all the temple tables together for brevity, including the Table of Showbread among them. In Ezekiel 40:39, eight tables of hewn stone are mentioned for slaughtering sacrificial victims. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 20 — Lampstands of Pure Gold

- **"The lampstands of pure gold and their lamps, to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as prescribed."** The lamps were to burn continually before the *debir* (inner sanctuary / Most Holy Place), according to the divinely prescribed ordinance. The Chronicler adds "as prescribed" (literally "according to the legal rule"), emphasizing continuity with the Mosaic instructions. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- The parallel in 1 Kings 7:49 adds "five on the right and five on the left," which the Chronicler omits here (having already given this detail in v. 7). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## v. 21 — Flowers, Lamps, and Tongs of Purest Gold

- **"The flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold — of purest gold."** The "flowers" refer to the floral decorative elements on the lampstands (almond blossoms, buds, etc., as in Exodus 25:31-36). The tongs were used for tending the lamps. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **"Of purest gold":** The Hebrew word *miklōth* ("perfections," an intensive plural) occurs nowhere else in the Bible. Ellicott calls it "a little touch, added to heighten the effect," quite in the manner of the Chronicler. It means "it was perfection of gold." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Frederick Mabie:** "The gold noted in conjunction with the altar utensils reflects their supreme importance in the sacrificial system. No expense was spared in even the smallest details." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]

---

## v. 22 — Wick Trimmers, Bowls, Ladles, Censers, and the Gold Doors

- **"The wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and censers of purest gold; and the gold doors…"** Every item associated with the temple service, down to the smallest utensil, was made of the finest gold. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **"Wick trimmers" (snuffers):** Shears or scissors for trimming the lamp wicks. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **The gold doors:** Both the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and the doors of the main hall (the Holy Place) were overlaid with gold. Frederick Mabie comments that "the gold doors of the temple, like the veil, were both works of art and functional means of protecting holy space." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary]
- **"Entry" vs. "hinges":** Ellicott discusses a textual question — 1 Kings 7:50 reads "hinges" (*pōthōth*), while Chronicles reads "entry" (*pethaḥ*). Ellicott argues against emending Chronicles to match Kings, since solid gold hinges are unlikely; it is more plausible that the *doors* themselves were plated with gold (1 Kings 6:32, 35). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Selman on the flora and fauna symbolism:** "The symbolism of flora and fauna in the temple may either indicate God's sovereignty over the created order or be another allusion to the harmony of all created things in God's presence as in the Garden of Eden." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ

### The Oxen vs. Gourds Question (v. 3)

This is primarily a textual-critical debate rather than a denominational one. Most Protestant commentators (Ellicott, Pulpit, and many modern scholars) assume a scribal error in Chronicles and prefer the Kings reading of "gourds." Ellicott is a notable exception, arguing both could be original. The Catholic Haydock commentary notes the discrepancy without resolving it definitively, acknowledging that the Septuagint and Syriac omit the verse entirely. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html] [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]

### The 3,000 vs. 2,000 Baths (v. 5)

No distinct *denominational* divide emerged on this point from the available sources. The range of explanations (different measures, usual vs. maximum capacity, scribal error) appears across traditions. The Catholic Haydock and the Targum both favor the "usual vs. maximum capacity" explanation. Evangelical sources like the *Defender's Study Bible* argue both numbers can stand as given. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary] [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]

### The Ten Tables vs. One Table (vv. 8, 19)

This is a classic synoptic difficulty between Chronicles and Kings. Ellicott suggests the Chronicler may have achieved "brevity at the cost of accuracy." Matthew Henry simply harmonizes: there were ten tables total, but one principal Table of Showbread. This is not a denominational dividing line but a harmonization question that all traditions address similarly. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-4.html]

### Typological Interpretations

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong Christological typology — the altar as cross, the Sea as cleansing through Christ, the twelve oxen as apostles carrying the water of life, the courts as the move toward universal priesthood. Application emphasizes generous, uncalculated giving to God. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-4/]
- **Reformed/Evangelical (Matthew Henry, Gaebelein):** Similar typological approach but with stronger emphasis on the "gospel privilege" of cleansing through Christ's blood and the duty of repentance. Gaebelein sees the entire temple as eschatological — foreshadowing the coming Kingdom of Christ. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-4-commentary] [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-4.html]
- **Catholic (Haydock):** More restrained on typology; focuses on historical and liturgical details — Josephus on the altar ascent, the comparison with post-exilic altar dimensions, the practical distinctions in priestly washing. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-4.html]

---

## What Was Not Found

- Specific Baptist (Spurgeon, DesiringGod, GTY), Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed, Wesley.nnu.edu), Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org), or Orthodox (OCA.org) commentaries on 2 Chronicles 4 were not returned in search results.
- Modern scholarly treatments (BibleOdyssey.org) and NET Bible notes were referenced indirectly via Precept Austin but direct pages were not retrieved.
- No prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teaching on 2 Chronicles 4 appeared in search results.
